Events.RelatedBody: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in Aspire. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components. Aspire Dashboard's unauthenticated NotFound route can permit telemetry deletion in both standalone and AppHost-hosted deployments. In standalone deployments using browser-token authentication, it can also expose the browser token. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/microsoft/aspire/issues/22148 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** Critical - **Score:** 9.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N` - **Weakness:** CWE-862 ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Any supported OS - **Architectures:** x64, Arm64 ## Affected Packages ### Standalone Aspire Dashboard Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- Aspire Dashboard | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 Both 13.6.3 and 13.6.4 contain the unauthenticated NotFound route. ### Aspire Dashboard SDK packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-musl-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-musl-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Aspire Dashboard releases through 13.6.4 are affected, whether deployed independently or launched by an Aspire AppHost. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, check the resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk package versions against the affected ranges above. If the AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, check the version of that Dashboard instead. Aspire ships independently of .NET; installing a .NET runtime or SDK update does not replace the Dashboard. ### How do I fix the issue? Update Aspire Dashboard to version 13.6.5 or later. Neither 13.6.3 nor 13.6.4 is a fixed upgrade target. For container deployments, explicitly set the Dashboard image to `mcr.microsoft.com/aspire/dashboard:13.6.5` and recreate or redeploy the container. Replace older version tags and nightly image references, including those in generated Docker Compose or Kubernetes manifests, with this fixed stable image. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace an image reference in an existing deployment manifest. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, update any explicit Aspire.Hosting.AppHost version, including a central package version, to 13.6.5 or later. If that reference is supplied implicitly by Aspire.AppHost.Sdk, update the SDK reference to 13.6.5 or later instead. Restore and rebuild the AppHost, verify that its resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk packages are 13.6.5 or later, and restart the AppHost to run the updated Dashboard. If your AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, update the Dashboard in that selected bundle or location to 13.6.5 or later and restart the AppHost. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace that Dashboard. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue in the Aspire repository at https://github.com/microsoft/aspire. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-118740](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-118740) ### Acknowledgements - Weeraphat Srisutham ### Revisions V1.0 (November 10, 2026): Advisory published.

## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in ASP.NET Core. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components. ASP.NET Core Identity scaffolding templates use the request-supplied email instead of the account's stored email for password-reset and confirmation messages. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/Scaffolding/issues/3959 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 (base score) - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-640 ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Any supported OS - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages Updating scaffolding packages/tools does not repair previously generated application code. Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc contains the affected templates. Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design is a parent package that brings in the MVC generator through a minimum-version dependency. For Design, applicability depends on the resolved MVC generator: a project that independently resolves a fixed MVC version does not become vulnerable merely because it retains an older Design reference. ### 8.0 - standalone packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.23 | 8.0.24 [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.23 | 8.0.24 ### 9.0 - standalone packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.12 | 9.0.13 [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.12 | 9.0.13 ### 10.0 - standalone packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) | >= 10.0.0, <= 10.0.2 | 10.0.3 [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design) | >= 10.0.0, <= 10.0.2 | 10.0.3 ### Additional known affected scaffolding prereleases These are exact known affected versions, not continuous prerelease intervals. Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold 20.3.0 Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold-aspnet has been incorporated into Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold. Version 20.3.0 supports .NET 8, 9, 10 and 11. Install it as a .NET tool, not as a project package reference. The MVC and Design project packages use the separate fixed versions listed above; 20.3.0 is not a version of those packages. ### Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold 20.x Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold) | >= 20.0.0-preview.1.26156.3, <= 20.1.0 | 20.3.0 The 20.x tool contains the vulnerable Identity and Blazor templates for .NET 8.0 through 11.0. ### Affected legacy prereleases The following exact versions also contain affected templates: - [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) and [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design): `11.0.0-preview.1.26156.3` and `11.0.0-preview.1.26230.3`. - [Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold-aspnet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold-aspnet): `10.0.0-rc.1.25458.5` and `10.0.0-rc.1.25468.1`. Apply the generated-code repair below to applications created with these versions. For new scaffolding, use the Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold 20.3.0 tool, which supports .NET 8 through 11. Migrating to that tool is not an update to an MVC or Design project package reference and does not repair previously generated code. ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Check both the installed scaffolding package/tool version and the code it generated. Applications generated with an affected template remain affected after the tool is updated unless their handlers are corrected. The `dotnet-aspnet-codegenerator` command loads generators from the application's dependencies. Check the project's Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design and Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc references against the versions above; updating only the command-line tool does not replace those project dependencies. For applications created with `dotnet new`, check the selected SDK with `dotnet --version` in the working directory. ## Description There appears to be a regression in the Razor source generator in .NET 11 involving nested type declarations inside a Razor component's `@code` block. When a Razor component contains a nested static class inside its `@code` block, the generated `.decl.g.cs` declaration for that component unexpectedly omits its base class. **This breaks component discovery for other Razor components inheriting from the affected component!** As a result: - **Derived Razor components are no longer recognized as components**. - Razor generates `OpenElement()` instead of `OpenComponent()` for references to those components. - RZ10012 warnings are reported for otherwise valid component references. - The Visual Studio Razor editor also fails to recognize these components, reporting them as unexpected markup elements and providing an incorrect editing experience. **This is a regression compared to .NET 10. The same source code and component inheritance hierarchy work correctly in .NET 10.** ## Minimal reproduction Consider the following component inheritance hierarchy: `WebsiteLayout` → `MasterLayout` → `GeneralLayout` ### WebsiteLayout.razor ```razor
Website layout
``` ### MasterLayout.razor ```razor @typeparam TModel @inherits WebsiteLayout @code { static class Foo { } } ``` ### GeneralLayout.razor ```razor @typeparam TModel @inherits MasterLayout
General layout
``` ### HomePage.razor ```razor ``` The critical part is the nested static class declared inside the `@code` block of `MasterLayout`. Removing the `@code` block makes the problem disappear. ## Actual behavior When the nested static class is present, the generated `MasterLayout_razor.decl.g.cs` contains a minimal class declaration **without its original base class**: ```csharp public partial class MasterLayout { } ``` When the nested static class is removed, the generated declaration correctly contains the base class: ```csharp public partial class MasterLayout : WebsiteLayout { } ``` This difference causes derived components to become invisible to Razor's component discovery mechanism. For example, the generated code for `HomePage` contains: ```csharp __builder.OpenElement(0, "GeneralLayout"); ``` instead of the expected component invocation: ```csharp __builder.OpenComponent>(0); ``` Razor consequently reports: ```text RZ10012: Found markup element with unexpected name 'GeneralLayout'. If this is intended to be a component, add a @using directive for its namespace. ``` The warning is not resolved by adding explicit `@using` directives or using fully qualified component names. ## Visual Studio editor impact This is not just a command-line build or runtime rendering problem. The Visual Studio Razor editor is affected as well. When the nested static class is present: - The editor fails to recognize derived components as Razor components. - Valid component references are marked with RZ10012. - Component markup is treated as unexpected markup rather than component invocations. - The editor's component recognition and associated editing experience are incorrect. Removing the nested static class restores component recognition in the editor as well as in the generated build output. ## Expected behavior Declaring a nested static class inside a Razor component's `@code` block should not affect the component's inheritance hierarchy or its identity as a Razor component. The generated declaration should preserve the component's base class, regardless of the presence of nested type declarations. Components inheriting from that component should continue to be discovered and compiled as Razor component invocations. The Visual Studio Razor editor should also correctly recognize these components without RZ10012 warnings. ## Regression | Version | Result | |---|---| | .NET 10 | Works correctly | | .NET 11 | Component inheritance discovery breaks when a nested static class is declared in `@code` | This has been reproduced using the same component definitions and inheritance structure, changing only the target .NET version. ## Additional observations The issue is specifically related to nested type declarations inside the Razor component's `@code` block. Other Razor-generated components can be inherited from without problems. The following workarounds have been tested: 1. Removing the nested static class restores correct component discovery. 2. Replacing the affected Razor component in the inheritance chain with an ordinary C# class restores correct component discovery. 3. Renaming the affected Razor component does not resolve the problem. 4. Explicit namespace imports and fully qualified component references do not resolve the problem. The generated declaration comparison strongly suggests that the issue is related to the Razor declaration/implementation splitting mechanism or its fallback handling of components containing nested types. In particular, the generated declaration loses the base class, which subsequently breaks component discovery for derived components. ## Environment - .NET SDK (working): 10.0.* - .NET SDK (failing): 11.0.100 - Target framework (working): `net10.0` - Target framework (failing): `net11.0` - Visual Studio version: Insiders 12409.143 - OS: Win 11

- **Alternatives / Unknowns:** The dumps and logs have not been analyzed, so a product deadlock, test-host/runtime failure, resource issue, or environment-specific condition remain possible.

3. If dumps do not identify the termination, compare target-branch behavior and obtain a diagnostic binlog or focused reproduction with host/runtime diagnostics.

- Matching prior build: [20261110.50](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/cbb18261-c48f-4abb-8651-8cdcb5474649/_build/results?buildId=1674681), same work item/mechanism on an independent commit

- **Mechanism fingerprint:** `test-execution|timeout|dotnet-watch.tests.dll.<n>|test-host-crashed-recovered-<n>-test-result-s-from-the-trx-streaming-sidecar-additional-results-that-were-in-flight-at-crash-time-may-be-missing-.-test-application-process-didn-t-e`

## Failure History

- Matching occurrence count: 2 observed builds: 1675206 (current, failed) and 1674681 (prior independent main-branch commit, failed).
- Surrounding sequence: 1672795 and 1672210 succeeded; 1673301, 1673580, 1673949, 1674455, 1674681, and 1675206 failed at the build level. The dossier establishes recurrence of this work-item mechanism in the current and 1674681 builds; it does not establish that every intervening build failed for the same mechanism.

## Error Details

Exact current observation excerpt:
`Test host crashed; recovered 93 test result(s) from the TRX streaming sidecar (additional results that were in flight at crash time may be missing). Test application process didn\u0027t exit gracefully, exit code is \u0027-1\u0027 [00:50:52] ServerAndResources`

The Helix work item reported exit code `7`; 89 tests passed and 93 results were recovered. Console: [console.e009ed57.log](https://helix.dot.net/api/jobs/4cfe0716-7bcd-4343-a833-8bda31691a07/workitems/dotnet-watch.Tests.dll.1/files/console.e009ed57.log?api-version=2019-06-17). Dump artifacts: [dotnet\_9384\_hang.dmp](https://helix.dot.net/api/jobs/4cfe0716-7bcd-4343-a833-8bda31691a07/workitems/dotnet-watch.Tests.dll.1/files/dotnet_9384_hang.dmp?api-version=2019-06-17), [WatchAspire\_1788\_hang.dmp](https://helix.dot.net/api/jobs/4cfe0716-7bcd-4343-a833-8bda31691a07/workitems/dotnet-watch.Tests.dll.1/files/Microsoft.DotNet.HotReload.Watch.Aspire_1788_hang.dmp?api-version=2019-06-17), [WatchAspire\_4324\_hang.dmp](https://helix.dot.net/api/jobs/4cfe0716-7bcd-4343-a833-8bda31691a07/workitems/dotnet-watch.Tests.dll.1/files/Microsoft.DotNet.HotReload.Watch.Aspire_4324_hang.dmp?api-version=2019-06-17), [WatchAspire\_6520\_hang.dmp](https://helix.dot.net/api/jobs/4cfe0716-7bcd-4343-a833-8bda31691a07/workitems/dotnet-watch.Tests.dll.1/files/Microsoft.DotNet.HotReload.Watch.Aspire_6520_hang.dmp?api-version=2019-06-17).

## Root Cause Analysis

- **Observed:** The test application did not exit gracefully while `ServerAndResources` was active; the test host crashed, dump files were written, and the TRX sidecar recovered results.
- **Assessment:** The immediate cause of the work-item failure is an abnormal test-host/application termination during test execution. The dossier does not establish why the process terminated; the generic `Monitor Helix Jobs` failure is a downstream parent, not the cause.
- **Confidence:** Medium for the immediate crash mechanism; Low for the underlying cause. Recurrence is supported by two independent main-branch builds, but recurrence alone does not establish flakiness or the crash trigger.
- **Alternatives / Unknowns:** The dumps and logs have not been analyzed, so a product deadlock, test-host/runtime failure, resource issue, or environment-specific condition remain possible.

## Suggested Investigation

1. Analyze the current and prior Helix dump files and console logs, comparing stacks and process/resource state at `ServerAndResources`.
2. Inspect the corresponding `dotnet-watch` test and recent build progression/changed files to determine whether a code change correlates with the recurrence.
3. If dumps do not identify the termination, compare target-branch behavior and obtain a diagnostic binlog or focused reproduction with host/runtime diagnostics.

Events.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "[Known Build Error] F# sample template snapshot mismatch after unversioned package update" (#57031) at dotnet/sdk
Events.RelatedBody:
## Build Information

Build: [1673143](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1673143)
Pull request: #57023
Failing test: `Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.New.IntegrationTests.TemplateEngineSamplesTest.TemplateEngineSamplesProjectTest`, case `06-console-csharp-fsharp`, `sample06 --language F#`.

The same snapshot mismatch fails on five legs: Linux x64, macOS arm64, macOS x64, Windows Core, and Windows FullFramework.

## Failure

The test [installs `Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Samples` without specifying a package version](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/fdaa8e87a7dcfc19b85e3826e2a8f9f83c36272a/test/dotnet-new.IntegrationTests/TemplateEngineSamplesTest.cs#L20). The original run passed this case; the rerun installed a newer samples package and failed against the unchanged checked-in snapshot.

The generated F# project now uses `Microsoft.NET.Sdk`, while the snapshot expects `FSharp.NET.Sdk;Microsoft.NET.Sdk` and additional legacy package references:

```diff
- <Project Sdk="FSharp.NET.Sdk;Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
+ <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
```

Template creation succeeds; snapshot verification fails. This is repeatable package/snapshot drift, not a template-engine hang or a trusted-root bundle regression. The historical hangs in #41795 are a different failure.

Evidence: [Linux x64 console](https://helix.dot.net/api/2019-06-17/jobs/9975eb17-15d9-4cb9-b4b7-9a9ce04c832f/workitems/dotnet-new.IntegrationTests.dll.11/console), [macOS arm64 console](https://helix.dot.net/api/2019-06-17/jobs/de399725-658f-40cb-9e57-39a2c05c7041/workitems/dotnet-new.IntegrationTests.dll.11/console), [macOS x64 console](https://helix.dot.net/api/2019-06-17/jobs/a00e2efb-3d04-4295-b431-6fd53c9e462f/workitems/dotnet-new.IntegrationTests.dll.11/console), [Windows Core console](https://helix.dot.net/api/2019-06-17/jobs/0a2be3b0-e05c-406c-9f24-5204ece4a17f/workitems/dotnet-new.IntegrationTests.dll.7/console), [Windows FullFramework console](https://helix.dot.net/api/2019-06-17/jobs/2bc4277e-6f6c-4d6f-8514-e00be466aeb0/workitems/dotnet-new.IntegrationTests.dll.7/console).

Suggested fix: pin the sample package to a version compatible with each branch's snapshots, or deliberately update the snapshots alongside a compatible package update.

## Error Message

The ordered messages match the specific SDK transition in the failing snapshot diff, without package versions, machine paths, or agent identifiers.

```json
{
  "ErrorMessage": [
    "- <Project Sdk=\"FSharp.NET.Sdk;Microsoft.NET.Sdk\">",
    "+ <Project Sdk=\"Microsoft.NET.Sdk\">"
  ],
  "BuildRetry": false,
  "ExcludeConsoleLog": false
}
```

Events.RelatedBody:
### Describe the bug

CA2007 reports an `await foreach` over an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` that has no `ConfigureAwait` call, but not one over `source.WithCancellation(cancellationToken)`. [`WithCancellation`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/313982dff3457c8291e8b88cd99785f6920319f0/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Threading/Tasks/TaskAsyncEnumerableExtensions.cs#L36-L41) creates its `ConfiguredCancelableAsyncEnumerable<T>` with `continueOnCapturedContext: true`, so that loop resumes on the captured context just like the unconfigured one.

The analyzer [skips any `await foreach` whose collection is a `ConfiguredCancelableAsyncEnumerable<T>`](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/88876b0c0b61b6e0ede17ac8e0ad8c95d3fc346b/src/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers/src/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers/Microsoft.CodeQuality.Analyzers/ApiDesignGuidelines/DoNotDirectlyAwaitATask.cs#L97-L99). `ConfigureAwait(bool)` and `WithCancellation(CancellationToken)` both return that type, so the type alone does not show whether the context was configured.

### Steps to reproduce

Create a class library with `dotnet new classlib --name Repro`, delete `Class1.cs`, and add this `.editorconfig` next to the project file:

```ini
root = true

[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2007.severity = warning
```

Add `Sample.cs`:

```csharp
namespace Repro;

public static class Sample
{
    public static async Task RunAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        await foreach (var item in source) { }
        await foreach (var item in source.WithCancellation(cancellationToken)) { }
        await foreach (var item in source.WithCancellation(cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false)) { }
    }
}
```

Run `dotnet build`.

### Expected behavior

CA2007 reports the first and second loops. The third loop calls `ConfigureAwait(false)`, so it is not reported.

### Actual behavior

CA2007 reports only the first loop:

```text
<repro>/Sample.cs(7,36): warning CA2007: Consider calling ConfigureAwait on the awaited task (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca2007)
```

### Is this a regression?

No. The `await foreach` check has skipped `ConfiguredCancelableAsyncEnumerable<T>` collections since dotnet/roslyn-analyzers#6683 added it.

### Are there any workarounds?

Write `.ConfigureAwait(false)` after `WithCancellation(...)` by hand. Nothing reports a loop where it is missing.

### dotnet --info output

Trimmed to the SDK, runtime environment, and host sections:

```console
.NET SDK:
 Version:           11.0.100
 Commit:            297acf930f
 Workload version:  11.0.100-manifests.08e30c08
 MSBuild version:   18.12.2-1.26529.118+297acf930

Runtime Environment:
 OS Name:     ubuntu
 OS Version:  26.10
 OS Platform: Linux
 RID:         linux-x64
 Base Path:   <dotnet-root>/sdk/11.0.100

Host:
  Version:      11.0.0
  Architecture: x64
  Commit:       297acf930f
```

### IDE version

None; reproduced with `dotnet build`.

### Other details

Telling the two calls apart means looking at the invocation chain that produced the collection, for example whether it contains a `ConfigureAwait` call, rather than at the collection's type.

dotnet/roslyn-analyzers#3703 is related: it asks for CA2007 to cover any type that has a `ConfigureAwait(bool)` method. This report is about a type the rule already handles.

```csharp
{
    public static async Task RunAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        await foreach (var item in source) { }
        await foreach (var item in source.WithCancellation(cancellationToken)) { }
        await foreach (var item in source.WithCancellation(cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false)) { }
    }
}
```

Run `dotnet build`.

### Expected behavior

CA2007 reports the first and second loops. The third loop calls `ConfigureAwait(false)`, so it is not reported.

### Actual behavior

CA2007 reports only the first loop:

```text
<repro>/Sample.cs(7,36): warning CA2007: Consider calling ConfigureAwait on the awaited task (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca2007)
```

### Is this a regression?

No. The `await foreach` check has skipped `ConfiguredCancelableAsyncEnumerable<T>` collections since dotnet/roslyn-analyzers#6683 added it.

### Are there any workarounds?

Write `.ConfigureAwait(false)` after `WithCancellation(...)` by hand. Nothing reports a loop where it is missing.

### dotnet --info output

Trimmed to the SDK, runtime environment, and host sections:


### IDE version

None; reproduced with `dotnet build`.

### Other details

Telling the two calls apart means looking at the invocation chain that produced the collection, for example whether it contains a `ConfigureAwait` call, rather than at the collection's type.

dotnet/roslyn-analyzers#3703 is related: it asks for CA2007 to cover any type that has a `ConfigureAwait(bool)` method. This report is about a type the rule already handles.

Issues.Title: [release/3.1] Reset current_no_gc_region_info after leaving no gc region implicitly
Issues.Body:
Backport https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/73602.

## Customer Impact
Customers reported occasional `System.InvalidOperationException` with message `The NoGCRegion mode was already in progress` when calling `GC.TryStartNoGCRegion`. This is preventing them from using this optimization and impacting their cold start latencies.

## Testing
Customers have tried the fix on .NET 6 overnight and reported the exception never appears again. Meanwhile, there is an unpatched machine and observed 72 exceptions of the same type in the same time interval, proving this does fix the bug.

## Risk
Low. This only impact customer using `TryStartNoGCRegion`, and this is the right thing to do.

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. > warning MSB3268: The primary reference "D:\a\1\s\iSAMS.Web.Controls\bin\Release\net48\iSAMS.Web.Controls.dll" could not be resolved because it has an indirect dependency on the framework assembly "netstandard, Version=2.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51" which could not be resolved in the currently targeted framework. Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions" (#1777)

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions" (#1786)

Issues.Title: linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem
Issues.Body:
Hello,

I am currently using .NET core 2.2.x and EF Core. 2.2.6. I have a function that returns a List<Animal> from the database with no issue. It returns 11 results. However, when I try to use `.Where(p => p.DeletedAt.GetValueOrDefault(DateTime.Now) => DateTime.Now).ToList()`, it still should return 11 results, however it returns 0. I also eliminated the possibility that there is something wrong with my where clause (logic) because it works perfectly on 4.6.1 EF Core 2.2.6. Furthermore, I confirmed that it is only where I am comparing a nullable type using that function and I am guessing that I missed a thread someone opened on this issue. I am aware .NET core 2.2 is not LTS. I also thought this goes here because it's not AFAIK, an EF core issue but rather an Ienumerable/Linq issue.

Update: As it turns out your notion of `DateTime.Now` getting evaluated twice is true. To rectify that, I will now be using `DateTime.Now.Date`. This is odd because this exact code works on 4.6.1. You're probably right. SMH. Thank you @GrabYourPitchforks! You may now close.

Issues.Title: Strong name signature not valid
Issues.Body:
Since I've ported a ClickOnce application from .NET Framework 4.6.1 to .NET Standard 2.0, the message _"Strong assembly name signature not valid for **Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll**"_ appears when trying to install or update the application. So the next step was to verify the assembly strong name by using the [Strong Name Tool](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/framework/tools/sn-exe-strong-name-tool) to make sure, that everything is fine, but:

```sh
> sn.exe -v Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll

Microsoft (R) .NET Framework Strong Name Utility Version 4.0.30319.0
Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll is a delay-signed or test-signed assembly
```

Additional information:

- The assembly versions `161.46041.41` and `161.46367.54` ended up in the same result
- This issue looks very similar to [this](https://www.damirscorner.com/blog/posts/20140502-StrongNameValidationFailedSecurityException.html)
- @markingmyname / @olprod: The root package, which is required for [Server Management Objects (SMOs)](https://docs.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/server-management-objects-smo/overview-smo?view=sql-server-ver15), is:
  - [Microsoft.SqlServer.SqlManagementObjects](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.SqlServer.SqlManagementObjects)
    - Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment
      - Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Authoring
        - **Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll**
- This issue appears on windows server machines but the software runs on different machines and I would like to avoid temporary workarounds such as editing the registry and activate the strong name bypass feature because of the forced validation on windows server machines

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Best Regards, Raphael --- ### Original Comments #### Raphael Affolter on 1/20/2020, 04:03 AM:

I forgot to mention: .Net Framework 4.6.1

Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.

**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Title: Better formatting of Html tags in Razor
Issues.Body:
In https://github.com/dotnet/razor/pull/12623 we made it so Razor "took over" Html indentation from the Html language service. Unfortunately, since 99% of our tests still provided html edits, a big focus of that work was ignoring some of edits that the Html language service wanted to make, and so I missed that in order to properly format Html, sometimes we have to construct our own edits.

Now that formatting is in `dotnet format`, which truly has no Html edits, and all of our tests run in that environment, there are gaps where our formatter doesn't do a good job. This fixes some of those gaps, particularly around tags that aren't the first thing on a line, and close tags. It mostly does this with some logic in (the increasingly badly named) `RazorFormattingPass`, which is nice since it doesn't introduce any new iterations through the tree, but for some edge cases there is a slight change in the C# pass too.

This also fixes https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/86396, therefore replaces https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86430, and makes part of #86308 apply in less scenarios, and all of that with better test outcomes IMO. At least ones that match VS/VS Code.

Issues.Title: Map old symbols to baseline
Issues.Body:
Map old symbols specified in SemanticEdit to the baseline when used for symbol mapping
The IDE creates SemanticEdits from the immediately preceding compilation (old) and the current compilation (new). The emit baseline however might be for an older generation than the immediately preceding generation. This occurs when no semantically significant changes are applied to the project while other projects are semantically changed. The entire solution advances to the next snapshot but baselines are emitted only for projects with significant changes.

If SemanticEdit.OldSymbol is used by the compiler for syntax offset mapping it is correct to use it as is.
If it is stored in various baseline maps or used for symbol mapping the compiler needs to map it to the baseline compilation beforehand.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/79898

Issues.Title: Fix Razor component discovery when a base component falls back
Issues.Body:
When a component can’t be split, its declaration shell has no base type. Components that inherit from it can then be missed during tag helper discovery.

Discover tag helpers from the full augmented compilation when any component falls back, rather than combining results from incomplete shells and fallback types.

This is probably the fix for https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/86444 but awaiting info from that user on the repro, before confirming.

It is definitely the fix for https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Razor-class-library-fails-to-build-after/11180609 / https://devdiv.visualstudio.com/DevDiv/_workitems/edit/3096913

@chsienki this is definitely your area of expertise, so if you have a better notion of how to do this instead of just using the full compilation when any component falls back, please let me know. Or feel free to put up your own PR as a replacement :)

Issues.Title: [Measurement only] Collect symbol completion wait durations
Issues.Body:
Temporary experiment to collect real build data for the 60-second symbol-completion timeout in dotnet/roslyn#86449. **Not intended to merge.** This branch includes that timeout change so CI exercises the same implementation.

- Unconditionally measure only incomplete waits, using the existing `Environment.TickCount` start timestamp and one additional read on exit. Already-completed calls do not allocate or access the accumulator.
- Aggregate by owning `CSharpCompilation`, with thread-safe duration buckets, outcome counts, accumulated wait milliseconds, and maximum wait milliseconds. No feature flag or process-global state; shared compilation remains enabled.
- Print one searchable `SymbolCompletionWaits:` summary per command-line compilation, including compilations with zero waits. Test compiler helpers capture the summary separately to preserve diagnostic-output assertions.

The `ms[0]` bucket means zero milliseconds measured, not a guarantee of sub-millisecond duration. Total wait time can overlap across threads and is not compilation wall time. Symbol-owner attribution also means waits on compilation references belong to the referenced compilation rather than necessarily the active request.

## Collecting results

Use the bootstrap-correctness build, which builds Roslyn with this PR compiler. Search the Build - Validate Correctness log or its published MSBuild binlogs for `SymbolCompletionWaits:`. Ordinary initial builds may use the SDK compiler and are not evidence of this instrumented path. Builds restored from the compilation-result cache do not execute the wait path or produce a fresh summary.

A local replay of the frozen C# compiler compilation successfully reported one completed wait at 36 ms. That is a smoke check, not a CI distribution or overhead measurement.

Issues.Title: Use a finite timeout for SpinWaitComplete
Issues.Body:
Follow up to #86367

I considered options for tracking which thread initiated work, and throwing immediately when that thread tries to wait on the results of that work. This had the following problems:
- Tracking this would add overhead, with additional concurrent collections, or ThreadStatics, etc., which may need to be allocated and accessed for each phase of symbol completion. That seemed significant to me.
- It could be done in debug mode only, perhaps, but I felt it would be useful for customers to be able to have things throw instead of hanging if they ever encounter these scenarios.

So I decided to just use a simple timeout in SpinWaitComplete instead. I chose 60 seconds as the timeout, to ensure that a busy CI machine would be very unlikely to timeout when the compiler is otherwise working correctly.

I had an agent do a spike in #86450, to get a sense of what kinds of waits occur in real CI builds. The results showed only a few hundred waits over an entire bootstrap build, and, most waits being shorter than the TickCount resolution (so less than ~15 ms). About 20% of waits were in the 15-100ms range. None were longer than that. This gives a strong sense that a legitimate 60+ second wait would be a pretty extreme outlier.

However, it seems difficult to be confident in reducing the timeout significantly, e.g. 5-10 seconds. Essentially we'd need to build confidence that so much time spent computing a result is a sign that things are broken.

I measured the perf overhead of this change in the build and wasn't able to observe any statistically significant difference in memory or elapsed time.

Issues.Title: Use Key Vault signing for the PR tagger
Issues.Body:
## Intent

Correct the GitHub App migration without moving private keys onto build agents. Keep WIF and short-lived installation tokens, read the configured App-ID secret projection for the JWT issuer, and sign only the SHA-256 digest through Azure Key Vault's RSA Sign operation.

The identifier contract is `appIdSecretName` / `AppIdSecretName` (`GitHubAppIdSecretName` for OneLoc), not a hardcoded App/Client ID in YAML. Only the App-ID projection is read. `keyName` selects the RSA signing resource; the private-key secret is never retrieved and there is no PEM/local-signing or PAT fallback.

## Scope and decisions

Updates the insertion issue-tagger caller to use dotnet-roslyn-issue-tagger-app-id and the proposed remote RSA key. The generated eng/common copy is intentionally untouched: this caller must wait for the corrected Arcade helper/template through normal dependency flow.

App-ID retrieval uses authenticated Key Vault REST and reads the response value directly. This avoids Azure CLI's Windows deserialization failure on the existing year-9999 secret expiry metadata; that workaround does not require exporting a private key.

The WIF identity requires read access to the configured App-ID projection and Sign on the selected RSA key, not read access to private-key secrets. No live credentials, keys, RBAC, production pipeline definitions or deployments were changed.

## Validation

- 98/98 mocked behavioral tests passed across four Arcade and three VS Code helper implementations, including the actual main VS Code inline YAML helper.
- Tests cover configured Client-ID/numeric-ID values, JWT signature/issuer/lifetime, denied/empty ID projections, Azure token/signing failures, installation paging/selection, GitHub failures and masking. Signing failure tests explicitly reject private-key retrieval/fallback.
- Both configured-ID success cases fail against the previous direct-ID helper for the intended hardcoded-issuer mismatch.
- 21 changed YAML files parsed; 24 PowerShell scripts/embedded scripts AST-parsed; all eleven worktrees passed `git diff --check`. Template expressions are substituted only in validation artifacts; this is not Azure DevOps template compilation.

## Gates before merging

Keep this PR **draft**. Protected canaries of the corrected remote-signing/App-ID-lookup code have **not run**. Validate actual WIF App-ID-read and Sign permissions, active GitHub key registration, and the real installation. Existing enabled key metadata is not proof of those checks.

The proposed release-tags, Roslyn tagger and VMR artifact-reader RSA key names were not returned by the prior key-list read and remain provisioning/registration blockers for their consumers. Monitor/Roslyn/VMR additionally require corrected Arcade dependency flow before merging their caller changes. Secret Manager PEM rotation does not synchronize RSA signing keys; establish coordinated rotation before retiring any in-use key.

Earlier VS Code canary3133371 and localization3133603 exercised local PEM signing, not these corrections. They do not satisfy the current protected validation gate.

Tracking: https://dev.azure.com/dnceng/internal/_workitems/edit/12467
Authoritative Arcade correction: https://github.com/dotnet/arcade/pull/17801

Issues.Title: IDE0072 (Populate switch) reports a false positive on an exhaustive switch over a `closed` class hierarchy
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: .NET 11.0.100 SDK, C# 15

**Steps to Reproduce**:

1. Save the following two files in an empty folder.

`.editorconfig`
```ini
root = true

[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0072.severity = warning
```

`repro.cs`
```csharp
#:property TargetFramework=net11.0
#:property EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true

public closed class Shape;
public sealed class Circle : Shape;
public sealed class Square : Shape;

public static class Describer
{
    public static string Describe(Shape shape) =>
        shape switch
        {
            Circle => "circle",
            Square => "square",
        };
}
```

2. Run `dotnet build repro.cs`.

**Diagnostic Id**: `IDE0072: Populate switch`

**Expected Behavior**: No diagnostic. Every direct descendant of the closed class is handled, so the compiler treats the switch as exhaustive. It reports no CS8509, and removing the `Square` arm does produce CS8509.

**Actual Behavior**:

```
repro.cs(16,15): warning IDE0072: Populate switch
```

IDE0072 appears to only recognise enums, so it doesn't know a closed hierarchy is complete. It should either skip switches over closed hierarchies, or recognise them and only report when a descendant is actually missing. The same may apply to switches over union types.

Issues.Title: [BUG] Nested static class in Razor @code block breaks component inheritance discovery in .NET 11 (Regression)
Issues.Body:
## Description There appears to be a regression in the Razor source generator in .NET 11 involving nested type declarations inside a Razor component's `@code` block. When a Razor component contains a nested static class inside its `@code` block, the generated `.decl.g.cs` declaration for that component unexpectedly omits its base class. **This breaks component discovery for other Razor components inheriting from the affected component!** As a result: - **Derived Razor components are no longer recognized as components**. - Razor generates `OpenElement()` instead of `OpenComponent()` for references to those components. - RZ10012 warnings are reported for otherwise valid component references. - The Visual Studio Razor editor also fails to recognize these components, reporting them as unexpected markup elements and providing an incorrect editing experience. **This is a regression compared to .NET 10. The same source code and component inheritance hierarchy work correctly in .NET 10.** ## Minimal reproduction Consider the following component inheritance hierarchy: `WebsiteLayout` → `MasterLayout` → `GeneralLayout` ### WebsiteLayout.razor ```razor
Website layout
``` ### MasterLayout.razor ```razor @typeparam TModel @inherits WebsiteLayout @code { static class Foo { } } ``` ### GeneralLayout.razor ```razor @typeparam TModel @inherits MasterLayout
General layout
``` ### HomePage.razor ```razor ``` The critical part is the nested static class declared inside the `@code` block of `MasterLayout`. Removing the `@code` block makes the problem disappear. ## Actual behavior When the nested static class is present, the generated `MasterLayout_razor.decl.g.cs` contains a minimal class declaration **without its original base class**: ```csharp public partial class MasterLayout { } ``` When the nested static class is removed, the generated declaration correctly contains the base class: ```csharp public partial class MasterLayout : WebsiteLayout { } ``` This difference causes derived components to become invisible to Razor's component discovery mechanism. For example, the generated code for `HomePage` contains: ```csharp __builder.OpenElement(0, "GeneralLayout"); ``` instead of the expected component invocation: ```csharp __builder.OpenComponent>(0); ``` Razor consequently reports: ```text RZ10012: Found markup element with unexpected name 'GeneralLayout'. If this is intended to be a component, add a @using directive for its namespace. ``` The warning is not resolved by adding explicit `@using` directives or using fully qualified component names. ## Visual Studio editor impact This is not just a command-line build or runtime rendering problem. The Visual Studio Razor editor is affected as well. When the nested static class is present: - The editor fails to recognize derived components as Razor components. - Valid component references are marked with RZ10012. - Component markup is treated as unexpected markup rather than component invocations. - The editor's component recognition and associated editing experience are incorrect. Removing the nested static class restores component recognition in the editor as well as in the generated build output. ## Expected behavior Declaring a nested static class inside a Razor component's `@code` block should not affect the component's inheritance hierarchy or its identity as a Razor component. The generated declaration should preserve the component's base class, regardless of the presence of nested type declarations. Components inheriting from that component should continue to be discovered and compiled as Razor component invocations. The Visual Studio Razor editor should also correctly recognize these components without RZ10012 warnings. ## Regression | Version | Result | |---|---| | .NET 10 | Works correctly | | .NET 11 | Component inheritance discovery breaks when a nested static class is declared in `@code` | This has been reproduced using the same component definitions and inheritance structure, changing only the target .NET version. ## Additional observations The issue is specifically related to nested type declarations inside the Razor component's `@code` block. Other Razor-generated components can be inherited from without problems. The following workarounds have been tested: 1. Removing the nested static class restores correct component discovery. 2. Replacing the affected Razor component in the inheritance chain with an ordinary C# class restores correct component discovery. 3. Renaming the affected Razor component does not resolve the problem. 4. Explicit namespace imports and fully qualified component references do not resolve the problem. The generated declaration comparison strongly suggests that the issue is related to the Razor declaration/implementation splitting mechanism or its fallback handling of components containing nested types. In particular, the generated declaration loses the base class, which subsequently breaks component discovery for derived components. ## Environment - .NET SDK (working): 10.0.* - .NET SDK (failing): 11.0.100 - Target framework (working): `net10.0` - Target framework (failing): `net11.0` - Visual Studio version: Insiders 12409.143 - OS: Win 11

Issues.Title: Stop counting a C# block in a script or style body twice when formatting Razor
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86441

With `razor_ignore_indentation_in_script_or_style_blocks_with_complex_razor = false`, a line inside a C# block in a `<script>` or `<style>` body moved one level deeper on every format. For example:

```razor
<script>
    @if (true)
    {
        @:value
    }
</script>
```

The first pass got it right. From the second pass on, `@:value` moved further right each time. The new tests show this happens on both the IDE and the dotnet format paths.

**Cause.** With the option off, `CSharpDocumentGenerator` honours each body line's existing indentation, less the enclosing Html elements. A line inside a C# block already has the block's level in that indentation, and the generated C# document also has a brace for the block, so the block was counted twice.

**The fix.** A line inside a C# block in the script or style body now takes its honoured indentation from the line that starts the outermost such block. The braces in the generated document indent the rest. A "C# block" here means a `CSharpCodeBlock` with statement literals; an expression such as `@Value` isn't one. The block's first line, and every line outside a block, are honoured exactly as before. So a block nested in JavaScript (an `@if` inside a `function`) stays at the JavaScript's level.

Not covered: Html or JavaScript text inside such a block is now indented by the braces, not by its own indentation. Before, the same double counting moved it further right on every run too.

Tests (in the shared `DocumentFormattingTest`, so each runs on the cohost and the dotnet format paths, all with the option off). In each one the input is the correctly formatted output and must come back unchanged:
- `CSharpBlockInScriptOrStyleKeepsIndentationWhenOptionDisabled`: `@:value` inside `@if`, in `<script>` and in `<style>`.
- `CSharpBlockInScriptKeepsIndentationWhenOptionDisabled_Legacy`: the same in a `.cshtml` file.
- `CSharpBlockInScriptFunctionKeepsIndentationWhenOptionDisabled`: the `@if` inside a JavaScript `function`.

The existing `UsesComplexRazorIndentationEditorConfig_Script/Style_False` tests are the first pass from unformatted input, and they still pass.

Mutation check: with `main`'s generator, all 4 new cases fail on both paths.

Idempotency: I ran the whole dotnet format suite with each output formatted a second time. The `@:value` cases no longer change on the second pass. The ones that still do are script and style bodies inside C# blocks under dotnet format (#86429, fixed by #86438) and multi-line lambdas in attributes (#86427, #86440).

This PR merges cleanly with #86438.

Results:
- **macOS:** `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat.UnitTests` passes 461 of 461. The cohost formatting tests pass, 705 passed and 1 skipped.
- **Windows (net472, with the WebTools `htmlFormatted` validation):** passes 891 of 891 on a [GitHub Actions run on my fork](https://github.com/Mpdreamz/roslyn/actions/runs/43195687284).

Issues.Title: Razor formatting indents a line inside a C# block in a script one level deeper on every run when ignoring complex script indentation is off
Issues.Body:
### Version Used

`main` at b907b90240f, through `RazorFormatter.TryFormatAsync` (the `dotnet format` entry point), with `indent_size = 4` and the shared test project's imports. Found while working on #86438.

### Steps to Reproduce

`.editorconfig`: `razor_ignore_indentation_in_script_or_style_blocks_with_complex_razor = false`

Format this `.razor` file, then format the result again:

```razor
<script>
    @if (true)
    {
    @:value
    }
</script>
```

### Expected Behavior

The first pass indents `@:value` under the `@if`, as `UsesComplexRazorIndentationEditorConfig_Script_False` expects. Later passes leave it there.

### Actual Behavior

Pass 1 is correct:

```razor
<script>
    @if (true)
    {
        @:value
    }
</script>
```

Pass 2:

```razor
<script>
    @if (true)
    {
            @:value
    }
</script>
```

Pass 3:

```razor
<script>
    @if (true)
    {
                @:value
    }
</script>
```

Each pass indents `@:value` one more level. `<style>` behaves the same way. With the option at its default (`true`), the block counts as complex Razor, its indentation is left as written, and the output doesn't change.

The cause is in `CSharpDocumentGenerator`. With the option off, every line of the script body keeps the indentation it already has, less the enclosing Html elements. For a line inside a C# block within the script, that indentation already includes the block, and the generated document has a brace for the block too. So the block's level is counted twice.

Issues.Title: Keep script and style bodies inside C# blocks in place when formatting Razor with dotnet format
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86429

Under dotnet format, the body of a multi-line `<script>` or `<style>` inside a C# block (`@if`, `@foreach`, `@section`, …) was indented one level deeper for each enclosing block, on every run. The formatter wasn't idempotent: formatting the output again moved the body further each time.

**Cause.** `CSharpDocumentGenerator` honours the Html formatter's indentation of script and style bodies. It takes each body line's indentation and subtracts the enclosing Html elements (`GetHtmlIndentationLevel`), because the generated C# document already has a brace for each of them. In the IDE that's correct: WebTools leaves elements inside C# blocks at column 0, so the text has no C# levels in it. dotnet format doesn't run an Html formatter, so the line still has its source indentation, and that includes the C# blocks. The generated document has braces for those too, so they were added a second time.

**The fix.**
- **A flag.** `FormattingEngineOptions.HtmlFormatterRan` defaults to `true`. `RazorFormatter`, the dotnet format entry point, sets it to `false`. The generator can't tell the two pipelines apart without it: both hand it a `SourceText`, and the dotnet format one just never went through an Html pass. The IDE path doesn't change.
- **Without an Html formatter, body lines are measured against the start tag's own indentation** instead of against its Html ancestors. The body keeps its position relative to the tag, wherever the C# formatter puts the tag. That needs no counting of C# constructs (`@if`, `else`, `@section`, templates, …), which would be easy to get wrong.

**Alternative I tried first.** I tried leaving body lines exactly as written (`processIndentation: false`). That's wrong for C# lines inside a script with the complex-Razor option off: `UsesComplexRazorIndentationEditorConfig_Script_False` expects `@:value` to be indented under its `@if`.

**Behaviour change at the top level.** When the start tag itself moves, the body now moves with it, the way WebTools shifts a script body as a whole in the IDE. Before, the body stayed where it was. Two existing dotnet format expectations change because of this:
- `DocumentFormatting_IndentsScriptBySpacesUsingEditorConfigIndentSize`: `<script>` moves from column 0 to column 2, and its body now moves with it.
- `Section_Scripts_ThreeScriptTags_HtmlFormatterDoesNothing_Expanded`: `<script>` moves from column 4 to column 0, and its body now moves with it.

**Existing expectations that recorded the bug.** These `dotNetFormatExpected` values (or the shared `expected`) had the body one level deeper than the input inside `@section`. They now come out unchanged apart from the tags the formatter already moved:
- `Section_ScriptBlock_PreservesHtmlFormatterIndentation`
- `Section_ScriptBlock_FormatsIncorrectJavaScriptIndentation`
- `Section_ScriptBlockInsideElement_PreservesHtmlFormatterIndentation`
- `Section_ScriptBlockInsideElement_FormatsIncorrectJavaScriptIndentation`
- `Section_ScriptBlockInsideMultipleElements_PreservesHtmlFormatterIndentation`
- `Section_StyleBlockInsideElement_PreservesHtmlFormatterIndentation`
- `Section_StyleBlockInsideElement_FormatsIncorrectCssIndentation`
- `Section_Scripts_ThreeScriptTags`
- `Section_Scripts_ThreeScriptTags_Expanded`
- `Section_Scripts_ThreeScriptTags_HtmlFormatterDoesNothing`

`Section_Scripts_ThreeScriptTags_HtmlFormatterDoesNothing` and `Section_Scripts_ThreeScriptTags_HtmlFormatterDoesNothing_Expanded` didn't have a `dotNetFormatExpected`, so they get one now. Their dotnet format output used to match the IDE's `expected` only because the body moved, from this bug in the first test and from the old top-level behaviour in the second.

**New tests** (in the shared `DocumentFormattingTest`, each one run with `ignoreIndentationInScriptOrStyleBlocksWithComplexRazor` both on and off):
- `ScriptBodyInIfKeepsIndentation`: the issue's repro.
- `ScriptBodyInIfKeepsIndentation_Legacy`: the same repro in a `.cshtml` file.
- `StyleBodyInNestedBlocksKeepsIndentation`: a `<style>` inside `@if` inside `@foreach`.
- `ScriptEndTagSharesBodyLineInIfDoesNotAffectFollowingContent`: `}</script>` inside `@if`, followed by more markup. This is the option-off `@if` case left out of #86428.

**Mutation check.** With `RazorFormatter` not setting the flag (the same as `main`), all 8 new cases fail on the dotnet format path, and so do the 12 updated tests. The cohost path isn't affected by the flag, so the new tests pass there on `main` too.

**Idempotency.** I ran the whole dotnet format suite with each output formatted a second time. On `main`, 30 cases change on the second pass. With this PR, 11 do, and none of them are script or style bodies inside C# blocks:
- **8 are multi-line lambdas in attributes**, such as `@onclick="()=>{` / `StateHasChanged();}"`.
- **3 are C# lines inside a script or style with the complex-Razor option off**, such as `@:value` inside `@if` inside `<script>`. The honoured indentation counts the inner `@if` twice in the same way.

This PR doesn't change either of those.

Results:
- **macOS:** `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat.UnitTests` passes 465 of 465. The cohost formatting tests pass, 709 passed and 1 skipped.
- **Windows (net472, with the WebTools `htmlFormatted` validation):** passes 895 of 895 on a [GitHub Actions run on my fork](https://github.com/Mpdreamz/roslyn/actions/runs/43191265561).

Issues.Title: Use Visual Studio's Tools > Options indent size when formatting Razor
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86431

Follow-up to #86307, which left out VS's separate Tools > Options indent size. `ClientSpaceSettings.IndentSize` was filled from `LANGPREFERENCES3.uTabSize`, so it held the tab size, and nothing read `uIndentSize`. In VS, with Tab size 4 and Indent size 2 and no `.editorconfig` `indent_size`, Razor indented by 4.

The change:
- **`ClientSpaceSettings`** is now `(IndentWithTabs, TabSize, IndentSize = null)`. The existing value is renamed to `TabSize` (JSON `tabSize`), since that's what it held. `IndentSize` (JSON `indentSize`) is the client's indent size, or `null` when the client doesn't report one. `Default` leaves it `null`.
- **`RazorLSPTextViewConnectionListener`** fills `IndentSize` from `uIndentSize`. The editor's own buffer and view options are unchanged: it still only sets the tab size and tabs/spaces there.
- **`GetRazorFormattingOptions`**: the indent size comes from `.editorconfig` `indent_size`, then the client's `IndentSize`, then the tab size, as before. With tabs, one level is still one tab.
- **VS Code** never sets `ClientSpaceSettings` (only the advanced settings), so `IndentSize` stays `null` there and it keeps indenting by the request's `tabSize`.
- **`ClientSettingsManager`** (VS) passes `TabSize` to `RazorGlobalOptions.TabSize`, as before.
- Existing tests that built `ClientSpaceSettings(…, IndentSize: n)` now say `TabSize: n`, which is what they meant.

Tests:
- `ClientIndentSizeFormattingTest` (cohost only, as dotnet format has no client settings): client indent 2 with tab 4 indents Html and `@code` by 2; `.editorconfig` `indent_size = 3` overrides the client's 2; with tabs, the client indent size is ignored and each level is one tab.
- `RazorEditServiceTest.NewMethod_NoCodeBlock_ClientIndentSize`: the edit service, which formats without an LSP request, indents by the client's 2.
- `RazorLSPTextViewConnectionListenerTest`: mocks `uIndentSize = 2` next to `uTabSize = 8`, and expects `ClientSpaceSettings(IndentWithTabs: true, TabSize: 8, IndentSize: 2)`.
- `ClientSettingsJsonSerializationTest`: round-trips `tabSize` and `indentSize`.

Results:
- **Mutation check:** without the client `IndentSize` fallback in `GetRazorFormattingOptions`, `IndentsBySpacesUsingClientIndentSize` and `NewMethod_NoCodeBlock_ClientIndentSize` fail; the `.editorconfig` and tabs tests pass either way, as they should. For the listener, on `main` the same mock with `uIndentSize = 2` sends `ClientSpaceSettings(true, 8)` ([run](https://github.com/Mpdreamz/roslyn/actions/runs/43187175418)), which the new expectation rejects.
- **macOS:** `Microsoft.VisualStudioCode.RazorExtension.UnitTests` 1972 passed, 3 skipped; `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Remote.Razor.UnitTests` 502 of 502; `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.Workspaces.UnitTests` 407 passed, 10 skipped; `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat.UnitTests` 457 of 457.
- **Windows (net472, `Microsoft.VisualStudio.LanguageServices.Razor.UnitTests`: formatting, edit service, listener, settings manager, generate method, inline completion and Roslyn code action tests, with the WebTools validation):** 961 passed, 1 skipped, on a [GitHub Actions run on my fork](https://github.com/Mpdreamz/roslyn/actions/runs/43188643860).

**Draft, because the VS side is unverified.** I can't run Visual Studio, so I haven't checked that:
- `GetUserPreferences4` for the Razor language service GUID returns the Tools > Options > Razor (ASP.NET Core) Indent size in `uIndentSize`;
- changing only the Indent size raises the view's `OptionChanged`, which is what makes the listener re-read the preferences (the listener test raises it for the tab size);
- VS's own editor features in Razor files (smart indent on Enter, which still comes from the buffer options) agree with the formatter afterwards.
